x-e-h3-01.title: Does an editorial's evidence reach all the way to its conclusion?
x-e-h3-01.topic: Editorial: reading the structure of an argument
x-e-h3-01.goal: In a short English editorial, find where the link between the evidence and the conclusion breaks, and rewrite the sentence to fit the range the evidence supports.
x-e-h3-01.material: This is part of an editorial in a local newspaper. Each line has a number.
x-e-h3-01.thinking.0: Examining how far the evidence goes
x-e-h3-01.thinking.1: Revising a conclusion to fit the range of the evidence
x-e-h3-01.prereq.0: Experience separating claims and reasons in a short English text
x-e-h3-01.prereq.1: Simple number expressions such as percentages and '9 out of 10'
x-e-h3-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that contains a part where the writer's evidence does not sufficiently support the conclusion.
x-e-h3-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately the group named in the conclusion and the group actually asked in the survey, and compare them.
x-e-h3-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether you can say the people who answered the survey are similar to all the people in the city.
x-e-h3-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the result of asking only 10 customers at one cafe, and line 4 widens it to 'most residents.' The problem is that we cannot know whether the people surveyed represent the whole city, so whether you chose line 3 (the range of the evidence) or line 4 (the widened conclusion), you looked at this link.
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite line 4 in English. Make it say only as much as the writer's evidence tells us.
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.hint.0: Decide first what to change in the sentence. Is it the group, the number, or the conclusion?
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write one sentence that means 'the evidence tells us only up to ....'
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Nine of the ten customers ...
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Who is your sentence talking about? Is it the same group that was actually asked in the evidence?
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Instead of just shrinking the conclusion, did you keep the writer's position (banning cars) and suggest adding other evidence?
x-e-h3-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It shrinks the conclusion and suggests the next step.

x-e-h3-02.title: Words you can check and words that appeal to the heart in a speech
x-e-h3-02.goal: In a student council candidate's speech, separate the information that can be checked from the emotional appeal, and evaluate whether it answers the opposing view.
x-e-h3-02.material:
This is part of a speech by Mina, a student council candidate promising to build a new library.
"Our school library has 6,000 books, but 40 percent of them are more than fifteen years old. Last year, 300 students borrowed more than ten books each. Some say we cannot afford a new library. But can we afford to let our dreams gather dust? Vote for a new library, and vote for our future."
x-e-h3-02.thinking.0: Separating statements that can be checked from appeals
x-e-h3-02.thinking.1: Judging what information a number needs to be meaningful
x-e-h3-02.thinking.2: Evaluating whether something answers a counterargument
x-e-h3-02.prereq.0: Experience reading an English speech once
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements that 'can be checked using only the information in the speech.'
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, find which sentence in the speech says it.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.hint.1: Separate what you can get by calculating from the numbers from the final appeal.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.r.a: This statement imagines and adds content that is not in the speech. You need to separate the information in the speech from your own guesses.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.r.b: This is a statement you can check from the number, 40 percent of 6,000.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.r.c: This is the final appeal of the speech, not confirmed information. You may have read information and appeal mixed together.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.r.d: You can check this from '300 students borrowed more than ten books each.'
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.r.e: The speech does not answer the cost issue. If you read it as if it answered the counterargument, you would choose this.
x-e-h3-02.s.s1.explain: b (about 2,400 old books) and d (some students borrowed a lot) can be checked from the numbers. c and e are only promised or hinted at by the speech with no evidence given, and a is not in the speech.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.prompt: To judge how strong '300 students borrowed more than ten books each' is as evidence that many students use the library, what do you need most?
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what standard makes the number 300 feel large.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the impression the same 300 students give in a school of 400 students and in a school of 3,000.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.r.a: The total number of loans helps, but you still cannot tell what share of all students the 300 are.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.r.b: You can judge how big the number 300 is when you compare it with the total number of students.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.r.c: Opening hours are information about convenience, and have little to do with whether 300 is a large number.
x-e-h3-02.s.s2.explain: You need to know what percent of all students the 300 are to judge whether it is 'many students.' A number only has meaning when there is something to compare it with.
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.prompt: Did the speech's "But can we afford to let our dreams gather dust?" answer the counterargument that 'we cannot afford a new library'? Write 1-2 sentences in English.
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one phrase what the counterargument was.
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.hint.1: Look at the speech again to see whether the question gives numbers or methods about the cost.
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly say 'what the counterargument was' in your answer?
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid making up facts that are not in the speech when evaluating?
x-e-h3-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: The same evaluation in different words.

x-e-h3-03.title: The same event, different headlines: judgments change as information grows
x-e-h3-03.goal: As information grows, revise your judgment of how a headline's tone and omissions tilt to one side compared with the facts, and explain one element in English.
x-e-h3-03.material: An article about a city council deciding to raise parking fees near the station is released in stages. Watch whether your judgment changes each time information grows.
x-e-h3-03.thinking.0: Understanding the impression made by word choice and omission
x-e-h3-03.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new information
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.prompt: The article's headline and content are revealed one piece at a time. At each stage, choose the most appropriate judgment using the information so far.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.hint.0: Separate the words in the headline that give facts from those that give a feeling.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.hint.1: First compare whether the new information changes your earlier judgment.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Headline: "Council Slaps Drivers with 50 Percent Fee Hike Near Station"
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What impression does this headline give the reader?
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.after: A word of judgment such as 'slaps' is laid over a fact (the fee goes up). At this point you have only grasped the impression.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A feeling that drivers are being punished unfairly
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 'Slaps' and 'hike' create an impression that makes drivers look like victims.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A feeling that the change is a small, everyday adjustment
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the opposite impression of a headline that uses strong words.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A feeling that the council has not decided yet
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The headline already says the fee was raised.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.info: First paragraph of the article: The hourly parking fee goes from 1,000원 to 1,500원, the first increase in 12 years. The council vote was 5 to 4.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the most appropriate evaluation of 'a 50 percent fee hike' and 'slaps' in the headline?
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The number is accurate. But the word 'slaps' and the omission of the context that the fee had not risen for 12 years tilted the impression to one side.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The number is wrong. The headline is false.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 1,000 to 1,500 is indeed a 50 percent increase. If you declare it false without checking the number, you end up here.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The headline is true, so it has no bias at all.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even if the numbers are right, the impression can change because of word choice and omission.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The number is right, but the word choice and the omission of 'first in 12 years' create a one-sided impression.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that checked the facts and evaluated the tone and omission separately.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Later in the article: The increased fees will be used for two new bus routes. The neighboring city charges 2,000원 per hour. The four council members who voted against said the increase was too large.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Given the facts known so far, which new headline is the fairest?
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.after: A fair headline uses only confirmed facts and leaves out words of judgment. Context such as the bus routes or the neighboring city's fee is the job of the body text.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is the bias of the other side, stressing only the good side and erasing the opposing view.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It contains only confirmed facts (the vote, the amount) and leaves out words of judgment.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 'Furious' makes up and attaches a feeling that is not confirmed in the article.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.info: Reader comment: "Every headline leaves something out, so there is no such thing as a fair headline."
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the most appropriate response to this comment?
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.after: Omission is unavoidable. So instead of 'biased or not,' it is more useful to compare 'which choice tilts more.'
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.o.a: True. Therefore all headlines are equally biased.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: 'Everyone omits things, so they are all the same' is a conclusion that gives up on comparing.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.o.b: False. A great editor could put all the facts in the headline.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: Headlines have a length limit, so they cannot include all the facts.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.o.c: It is partly true, but some choices tilt more to one side than others.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: This is a judgment that accepts both that omission is unavoidable and that there are differences of degree.
x-e-h3-03.s.s1.reflect: When you saw only the first headline, you could only grasp the impression, and after checking the facts you could evaluate the numbers and the tone separately. When new information comes, you revise the judgment 'this headline is biased' by splitting it into numbers, words and omission.
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.prompt: Pick one word or omission that makes the first headline (Council Slaps Drivers ...) look tilted to one side, and explain it in English.
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.hint.0: First pick one word in the headline that gives a feeling.
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write in one sentence how the reader's impression would change if that word were removed.
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain that the word or omission you chose changes the 'impression,' not the facts?
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: If you chose an omission, did you write specifically what was left out?
x-e-h3-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It points out both the word and the omission.

x-e-h3-04.title: The same facts, two readers: filtering out judgment words and rewriting
x-e-h3-04.goal: Separate facts from evaluation in a sentence mixed with judgment, and rewrite it in English for different readers: a neutral article for the school website and a notice for parents.
x-e-h3-04.material:
A school newspaper printed this sentence. "The principal's harsh new rule steals students' phones every morning, and parents are rightly angry."
The facts are as follows. From March 4, students put their phones in a storage box at 8:30 a.m. and get them back at 3:30 p.m. One parents' group asked the school to review the rule. The school explained that the rule is to help students focus in class.
x-e-h3-04.thinking.1: Adjusting the tone for the reader
x-e-h3-04.prereq.1: Experience seeing the basic frame of an English email or notice
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions in the sentence above that contain the 'writer's judgment,' not 'facts.'
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the facts (what, when) stay the same even if you remove that word.
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.hint.1: Sort them by 'can anyone confirm it, or is it someone's evaluation?'
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.r.a: 'New rule' tells the fact that a rule is starting. It is a description, not a judgment.
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.r.c: This describes the time students hand in their phones, so it is close to a fact.
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.r.d: 'Steals' is an evaluation that compares storing the phones to theft.
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.r.e: 'Rightly angry' is an expression in which the writer judges that the anger is justified.
x-e-h3-04.s.s1.explain: Harsh, steals and rightly angry carry the writer's evaluation, not facts. New rule and every morning are descriptions.
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.prompt: Write a neutral article sentence in English for the school website. It should include the facts (the time, the phones, the parents' request) and leave out the judgment words.
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put each of the three given facts into your sentence one by one.
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.hint.1: Take the evaluation words out of the original sentence, and fill in the facts on the skeleton that remains.
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check one by one that only 'facts anyone can confirm' remain in your sentence?
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether even a polite-looking adjective like 'strict' contains a judgment?
x-e-h3-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: It uses the time as a range.
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.prompt: This time, write the same content in English as a notice to parents. Begin politely and include the school's reason.
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.hint.0: First decide what parents would be most curious about.
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.hint.1: Add a sentence explaining the school's reason after the fact sentences.
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: What changed compared with the website article (the greeting, the softer expressions, the reason)?
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: While adding polite expressions, did you keep the facts (the times, the start date)?
x-e-h3-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It includes both a request and thanks.

x-e-h3-05.title: Does '9 out of 10' tell us about the whole school?
x-e-h3-05.goal: By making a survey result that looks convincing yourself, explain why a small survey weakly supports a claim about the whole school.
x-e-h3-05.material: Jun said, "Most of our 1,200 students like the new lunch menu. I asked my friends, and 9 out of 10 said yes."
x-e-h3-05.thinking.0: Separating the size of a number from the strength of evidence
x-e-h3-05.thinking.1: Making examples that serve as counterexamples
x-e-h3-05.thinking.2: Explaining the limits of a survey method
x-e-h3-05.prereq.1: Simple English sentences about survey results
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.prompt: What should you check first before believing Jun's claim?
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write Jun's number and the group in the claim (the whole school) side by side.
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what kind of survey method would make the same result hard to believe.
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.r.a: The menu price is interesting information, but it is not directly related to how far to trust the survey result.
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.r.b: Whom you asked and how many you asked decides how far the result can be extended to the whole school.
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.r.c: Comparing with last year shows change, but it does not tell you whether this survey is trustworthy.
x-e-h3-05.s.s1.explain: Whether the result represents the whole school depends on the number and the selection method of the people surveyed. You cannot tell from the fact that the percentage is high.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.prompt: Make two different survey results where more than 60 percent answered 'like,' which look convincing, but where 20 or fewer students were surveyed. (n = number of students surveyed, y = number of students who answered 'like')
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on one number: to be over 60 percent, how many responses out of the number surveyed would be needed?
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.hint.1: Change the number surveyed and match the number of responses.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.hint.2: You need to make two with different numbers of students.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of students is a suitable whole number.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of students surveyed must be a whole number of 1 or more, and the number of responses must be a whole number from 0 up to the number surveyed.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.ok.c2: 'Like' is more than 60 percent of the total.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c2: 'Like' responses do not exceed 60 percent of the number surveyed.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The number surveyed is 20 or fewer.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The number surveyed is more than 20.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.explain: Even with a high ratio like 4 out of 5 (80 percent) or 9 out of 12 (75 percent), it is a very small group compared with the 1,200 students in the whole school. Even with the same ratio, the strength of the evidence depends on how many people were surveyed and how.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain in English why a result like this (for example, 8 out of 10) only weakly supports a claim about all 1,200 students, and what you would change to make a better survey.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the number of people asked with the number of students in the whole school.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: If you asked only friends, think about whether those friends are similar to the whole school.
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you separate 'the number is small' from 'the people asked may not be representative' in your explanation?
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you specifically write how to fix it (more people, random selection, and so on)?
x-e-h3-05.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It covers both the representativeness problem and the improvement.

x-e-h3-06.title: Students who eat breakfast have higher grades: what else do we need to know?
x-e-h3-06.topic: strength of evidence: correlation and cause
x-e-h3-06.goal: Judge whether a survey result tells us about the 'cause,' choose the extra information needed for that judgment, and write in English a question to ask the researcher.
x-e-h3-06.material:
This is a claim from a school article. "Students who eat breakfast get higher test scores, so the school should provide free breakfast." As evidence, the results of a survey of 200 students were presented like this.

Group | Number of students | Average score
Students who eat breakfast | 130 | 82
Students who skip breakfast | 70 | 74
x-e-h3-06.thinking.1: Telling which extra information is useful
x-e-h3-06.prereq.1: Experience making English questions (Did / Has / Do ... ?)
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.prompt: What information is needed to judge the conclusion 'free school breakfast raises scores'? Choose all that fit.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether each piece of information helps answer the question, 'Is the relationship between breakfast and scores a cause?'
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one reason the conclusion could be wrong, and find the information that would check it.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.r.a: Favorite menu items are information that has almost nothing to do with the conclusion.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.r.b: This is a question that checks whether there are other differences, besides eating breakfast, that could affect scores.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.r.c: This is a question that looks for cases that directly tested the cause.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.r.d: Operating hours are information about carrying it out, not evidence of an effect.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.r.e: To compare scores, they must have been measured on the same standard.
x-e-h3-06.s.s1.explain: b (other causes: sleep, study time), c (the results of actually doing it) and e (the fairness of the comparison) help confirm it. a and d have almost nothing to do with whether the conclusion is right.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.prompt: What is the most appropriate conclusion you can state from the table alone?
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.hint.0: Separate what the numbers in the table say from the interpretation of the reason.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.hint.1: If the conclusion sentence contains 'because' or 'if ... then,' check whether the table shows that too.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.o.a: Students who eat breakfast had higher scores, but we do not know why
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.r.a: This judgment says only the facts the table shows and leaves the cause open.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.o.b: If free school breakfast is started, the school's average score will rise
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.r.b: The table only compares students who eat breakfast with students who do not, and does not show the result of providing breakfast.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.o.c: Breakfast has nothing to do with grades
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.r.c: Saying there is no relationship when the table shows a difference does not match the table.
x-e-h3-06.s.s2.explain: The table only shows the difference in averages between the two groups and does not prove a cause. To talk about a cause, you need more information that rules out other explanations.
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.prompt: Write in English one sentence of a question to send to the researcher who did this survey. A question that targets a weakness of the conclusion above would be good.
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.hint.0: If the conclusion could be wrong, what other reasons could create the score gap?
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.hint.1: Turn that reason into a Yes/No question to check it.
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is your question one where even a yes or no answer would change how much you believe the conclusion?
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid asking again about information that is already in the table?
x-e-h3-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It asks about cases that directly tested the cause.

x-e-h3-07.title: Writing a rebuttal paragraph that answers the other side's claim
x-e-h3-07.goal: Write a rebuttal to the claim to abolish school uniforms that partly concedes and then argues back with reasons, and also write an answer to an expected counter-rebuttal, in English.
x-e-h3-07.material: The claim for a debate topic: "School uniforms should be abolished because they limit self-expression." Write a rebuttal to this claim. Whichever side you take, you must give reasons, and it is fine if it differs from your real opinion.
x-e-h3-07.thinking.0: Separating a rebuttal from simple disagreement
x-e-h3-07.prereq.0: Writing English sentences that link reasons with although, because and so on
x-e-h3-07.prereq.1: Any experience of doing a for-and-against debate in English
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most appropriate 'rebuttal' to the claim above?
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether each choice is related to the reason 'self-expression is limited.'
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether each choice accepts the other side's reason, argues against it, or shows something else that matters.
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.r.a: It answers the reason the other side gave (self-expression) with other benefits and alternatives.
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.r.b: It does not answer the claim's reason (limited self-expression) and only mentions other advantages.
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.r.c: The reason 'many people do it, so it's right' does not answer the self-expression issue.
x-e-h3-07.s.s1.explain: A rebuttal has to respond to the reason in the other side's claim. Simply stating the opposite position or other advantages is not enough.
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.prompt: Write a rebuttal paragraph (2-3 sentences) in English to the claim above. First concede part of the other side's claim, then argue back with a reason.
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.hint.0: First decide which part of the other side's claim you can admit is right.
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.hint.1: After conceding, continue with 'however' or 'but' and write your reason.
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the part you conceded a part that is really right, not a weakened imitation of the other side's claim?
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your reason directly connected to the other side's reason, 'self-expression is limited'?
x-e-h3-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: It concedes and gives a reason.
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.prompt: Anticipate the strongest counter-rebuttal the other side could make to your rebuttal, and write in English a sentence that answers it.
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.hint.0: First look for the weakest part of your rebuttal.
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.hint.1: From the other side's position, attack that part in one sentence, and then answer it.
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Some students might say ... Even so, ...
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the counter-rebuttal you anticipated really target a weak spot in your rebuttal?
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your answer take up the counter-rebuttal and argue back, instead of ignoring it?
x-e-h3-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: It answered a different counter-rebuttal using the same structure.

x-e-h3-08.title: An email asking the teacher for a deadline extension
x-e-h3-08.goal: Find which words in a draft sound like a command, rewrite it as a polite email asking the teacher, and infer the hidden meaning of the reply.
x-e-h3-08.material: The essay deadline is Friday, but you want to hand it in two days late because of school festival practice. This is a draft a student wrote to send to the English teacher, Mr. Lee.
x-e-h3-08.thinking.0: Judging the impression a tone gives
x-e-h3-08.thinking.2: Inferring the hidden meaning of indirect expressions
x-e-h3-08.prereq.0: Basic email expressions such as Dear ~, and Thank you
x-e-h3-08.prereq.1: Experience seeing requests made with could and would
x-e-h3-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line that could sound to the teacher like a command, not a request.
x-e-h3-08.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and check whether it sounds to the other person like an order ('do it') instead of a request ('please do it').
x-e-h3-08.s.s1.hint.1: Which line could be changed to 'Could you ...?' with the same content?
x-e-h3-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 (Give me ...) and line 4 (Reply today.) are in the imperative form, as if giving orders to the teacher. The Hey in line 1 and the Bye in line 5 are casual, the way you speak to a friend, which is a pity, but the goal of this question is to find the lines that sound like commands.
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the draft in English as a polite email to the teacher. Include a greeting, a soft request, a reason, and thanks.
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.hint.0: Look for an expression that can turn 'Give me ...' into a question.
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.hint.1: Decide the order of the email (greeting - request - reason - thanks) and write one part at a time.
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you change the request sentence into a question or a hypothetical expression instead of 'Give me'?
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the reason reads as an explanation of the situation and not an excuse?
x-e-h3-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: It has a request in question form and thanks.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.prompt: Mr. Lee replied like this. "Fine, but I hope this won't become a habit." What is the most reasonable thing to infer from this reply?
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.hint.0: Read the first part and the last part of the reply separately and see what each says.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how a sentence starting with 'hope' is different from a direct command.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.r.a: You read 'Fine' (permission) and 'hope ... won't become a habit' (a wish that it not be repeated) together.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.r.b: You may have missed the word 'Fine' and read only the warning that follows.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.r.c: There is no direct expression of being angry. This is an inference that reads too much emotion into it.
x-e-h3-08.s.s3.explain: The reply accepts the request while carrying the hidden meaning of not repeating it. A remark like this does not directly say 'not in the future' but gently conveys an expectation.

x-e-h3-09.title: A complaint that is polite but doesn't get across
x-e-h3-09.goal: Choose complaint expressions that are both polite and clear, infer from the hidden meaning of softened remarks, and explain why an overly roundabout expression is less effective.
x-e-h3-09.material: The coffee you ordered at a cafe still hasn't come after 40 minutes. You are going to speak to the staff.
x-e-h3-09.thinking.1: Inferring hidden meaning from indirect expressions
x-e-h3-09.thinking.2: Explaining the effect of an expression
x-e-h3-09.prereq.0: Basic request expressions such as Excuse me, and Could you ...?
x-e-h3-09.prereq.1: Experience ordering at a cafe in English
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions to say to the staff that are polite and also clearly convey what you want them to do.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.hint.0: Evaluate each expression separately on two questions: 'Is it polite?' and 'Is what the staff must do clear?'
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.hint.1: Keep only the ones that satisfy both.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.r.a: It is clear but not polite enough, so the staff may react defensively.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.r.b: It conveys the situation and the request clearly and politely.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.r.c: In trying to be polite, the request became blurry. The staff may not notice there is really a problem.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.r.d: It does not convey the complaint at all, so the staff has no reason to take action.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.r.e: It expresses an apology while making clear what you are asking them to do.
x-e-h3-09.s.s1.explain: b and e are polite while making both the situation (ordered 40 minutes ago) and the request (please check) clear. a lacks politeness, c lacks clarity, and d lacks a request.
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.prompt: You asked a professor, "Could you look at my draft today?" and the professor replied, "I'm afraid I'm away until Friday." What is the most reasonable inference from this reply?
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.hint.0: See how the information in the reply (away, until Friday) connects to today's request.
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.hint.1: Separate what the professor said from what you added by guessing.
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.r.b: The professor never said she would read it on Friday. It adds a promise that was not made.
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.r.c: It reads both the hidden meaning that today is hard and the possibility that the refusal is not permanent.
x-e-h3-09.s.s2.explain: The professor only gave the reason that today is not possible. The next thing to do is to politely ask again about a time that works.
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.prompt: Explain in 1-2 English sentences why option c from question 1 is weak even though it looks polite.
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.hint.0: Read c and see whether the staff can find something they need to do.
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.hint.1: See how words like 'maybe,' 'possibly,' and 'probably nothing' change the strength of the request.
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation say 'the request does not get across' instead of saying 'politeness is the problem'?
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you imagine what you would have to do if you heard that sentence as the staff?
x-e-h3-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: The same explanation in different words.

x-e-h3-10.title: A message where you can't tell who 'she' is
x-e-h3-10.goal: Find a sentence in a group message that can be read two ways, rewrite it so each meaning can be read only one way, and judge when the ambiguity is not a problem.
x-e-h3-10.material: These are messages from a group chat for preparing for a science festival. Each line has a number.
x-e-h3-10.thinking.2: Judging how serious a problem is depending on the situation
x-e-h3-10.prereq.0: How English pronouns (she, her) are used
x-e-h3-10.prereq.1: Indirect speech sentences (She told me that ...)
x-e-h3-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that different readers could understand differently.
x-e-h3-10.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, check whether you can fix 'who does what' as one thing.
x-e-h3-10.s.s1.hint.1: In the lines with pronouns, count how many people each pronoun could refer to.
x-e-h3-10.s.s1.explain: The 'she' in line 2 could refer to Ms. Han or to Ms. Seo. So who has to book the hall can be read two ways. The other lines can be read in only one way as to who must do what.
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.prompt: Write in English the two meanings line 2 could have, each as a sentence that can be read only one way. (Write two sentences.)
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write down separately the case where 'she' is Ms. Han and the case where 'she' is Ms. Seo.
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.hint.1: If you use quotation marks as if quoting directly instead of a pronoun, it becomes clear who is speaking.
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Ms. Han told Ms. Seo, "..."
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can a person reading each of your two sentences understand it in only one way?
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did the sentence stay natural without using a pronoun?
x-e-h3-10.s.s2.modelNote.1: Instead of a direct quote, it made things clear by repeating the name and using a reflexive pronoun.
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.prompt: In which case would sending the original sentence (Ms. Han told Ms. Seo that she had to book the hall.) as it is not be a big problem?
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whether the readers can learn from somewhere other than this message who is booking.
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.hint.1: What condition must the readers meet for the ambiguity to cause harm?
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.o.a: When sending it to a group chat that many people read quickly
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.r.a: The more readers there are and the faster they read, the more likely a misreading becomes.
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.o.b: When an exclamation mark is attached at the end of the sentence
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.r.b: Punctuation cannot change whom a pronoun refers to.
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.o.c: When everyone already knows who is booking
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.r.c: This is a case where information from the situation resolves the ambiguity instead.
x-e-h3-10.s.s3.explain: Ambiguity is a problem of the text itself, but if the readers already know the information, the harm is smaller. For many readers who do not have the information, it must be fixed.
